Problem note

Irrationality criteria for Lambert subseries

Erdős #257 26 pp By Will Cook 30 September 2026
PDFOpen the PDF · 26 pp TeXLaTeX source Source on GitHub Problem dossier

Précis

For a finite nonempty set P of primes, let h(a) be the P-part of a. If ∑𝑎∈𝐴ℎ(𝑎)/(𝑎(2ℎ(𝑎) −1))∑a∈Ah(a)/(a(2h(a)−1)) is finite, then ∑𝑎∈𝐵(𝑏𝑎 −1)−1∑a∈B(ba−1)−1 is irrational for every integer 𝑏 ≥2b≥2 and every infinite B⊆A. The condition permits a divergent reciprocal sum, but excludes full support and all odd exponents. The proof averages positive displacements over multiples of a finite modulus; a second, dyadic average controls incomplete periods. The paper also proves the reciprocal-summable criterion stated by Erdős and a common-average extension using positive divisor covers. Supplementary results concern finite denominators and conditional rational-membership tests, not a resolution of the universal problem.

This paper owns problem-specific mathematical exposition for Erdős #257: exact finite-prime weighted support criterion, mixed weighted-and-cover support theorem and their ordinary proofs, exact finite periods, settled support families, method limits, and the open half-value edge.

It is not authority for the validity of claims tagged Lean, which belongs to the cited kernel-checked source, or a solution to Erdős #257, which remains open.

Authorship and AI use. Will Cook built and directed the research infrastructure and maintains the public release. He reviewed claims when he could. AI agents did most of the research and drafting. Cook did not independently verify every claim.

Cite and contact. Cite this paper by its title, author and date above, with its PDF; cite the earlier sources it uses for a mathematical result. For software, use the release citation and give the commit used. Contact Will with questions or corrections.

Introduction

For a set 𝐴A of positive integers and a real number 𝑏 >1b>1, write

𝑋𝐴(𝑏)=∑𝑎∈𝐴1𝑏𝑎−1.XA(b)=∑a∈A1ba−1.

This series converges by comparison with a geometric series, since (𝑏𝑎 −1)−1 ≤𝑏1−𝑎/(𝑏 −1)(ba−1)−1≤b1−a/(b−1). Erdős proved irrationality for full support at integer bases [5], and later proved the same conclusion for pairwise coprime supports of finite reciprocal sum [7]. On that page he stated that the coprimality assumption could be removed, without giving the details. The question for arbitrary infinite support in base two is Problem #257:

Problem 1.1 (Erdős #257). Is 𝑋𝐴(2)XA(2) irrational for every infinite 𝐴 ⊆ℕ>0A⊆N>0?

The conditions below are hereditary: if a set satisfies one of them, so does each of its infinite subsets. For the first condition, consider an exponent 𝑎 =2𝑘𝑚a=2km with 𝑚m odd. We replace its reciprocal weight 1/(2𝑘𝑚)1/(2km) by 1/[𝑚(𝑏2𝑘 −1)]1/[m(b2k−1)], so that a large power of 22 in 𝑎a reduces its contribution to the sum. More generally, for a finite set 𝑃P of primes, let the 𝑃P-part of 𝑎a be ℎ(𝑎) =∏𝑝∈𝑃𝑝𝑣𝑝(𝑎)h(a)=∏p∈Ppvp(a), where 𝑣𝑝(𝑎)vp(a) is the exponent of 𝑝p in 𝑎a.

Theorem 1.2 (a weighted condition on the support). Let 𝑏 ≥2b≥2 be an integer, let 𝐴 ⊆ℕ>0A⊆N>0 be infinite, and let 𝑃P be a finite nonempty set of primes. Set ℎ(𝑎) =∏𝑝∈𝑃𝑝𝑣𝑝(𝑎)h(a)=∏p∈Ppvp(a). If

𝑊𝑏,𝑃(𝐴):=∑𝑎∈𝐴ℎ(𝑎)𝑎(𝑏ℎ(𝑎)−1)<∞,(1)(1)Wb,P(A):=∑a∈Ah(a)a(bh(a)−1)<∞,

then 𝑋𝐴(𝑏)XA(b) is irrational. In particular, the base-two condition

∑𝑎∈𝐴ℎ(𝑎)𝑎(2ℎ(𝑎)−1)<∞(W)(W)∑a∈Ah(a)a(2h(a)−1)<∞

implies that 𝑋𝐴(𝑏)XA(b) is irrational for every integer 𝑏 ≥2b≥2. Both conclusions are hereditary under passage to infinite subsets.

Consider the support

𝐴⋆={2𝑘𝑚:𝑘≥1, 𝑚 odd, 𝑚≤22𝑘}.A⋆={2km:k≥1, m odd, m≤22k}.

For a fixed 𝑘k, the sum of 1/𝑚1/m over the odd cofactors is of order 2𝑘2k. Thus the corresponding terms contribute at least 1/41/4 to ∑𝑎∈𝐴⋆1/𝑎∑a∈A⋆1/a, but at most 21−𝑘21−k to (W). The calculation in Section 2 proves both bounds. Every infinite subset of 𝐴⋆A⋆ consequently gives an irrational value at every integer base. Since ℎ/(2ℎ −1) ≤1h/(2h−1)≤1, the same theorem also includes reciprocal-summable supports. Section A gives a direct proof of Erdős’s stated extension.

The divisor-cover condition instead bounds fractional powers of finite divisor counts by positive sums over divisors (Theorem 3.1). We prove that the two conditions are incomparable and that their union gives a further irrationality criterion: if 𝐸E satisfies the weighted condition and 𝑉V has a summable divisor cover, every infinite subset of 𝐸 ∪𝑉E∪V has irrational sum (Theorem 4.1). The separating constructions in Proposition 5.1 then give a union outside both individual classes (Corollary 5.2). These are sufficient hypotheses for Problem 1.1; the arbitrary support in that problem need not satisfy them.

The proofs compare a multiple of 𝑋𝐴(𝑏)XA(b) with an integer. For a positive integer 𝑁N, put

Δ𝑏,𝐴(𝑁)=∑𝑎∈𝐴𝑏𝑁mod𝑎−1𝑏𝑎−1=(𝑏𝑁−1)𝑋𝐴(𝑏)−𝐽𝑏,𝐴(𝑁),𝐽𝑏,𝐴(𝑁)=∑𝑎∈𝐴𝑎≤𝑁⌊𝑁/𝑎⌋∑𝑗=1𝑏𝑁−𝑗𝑎.(D)(D)Δb,A(N)=∑a∈AbNmoda−1ba−1=(bN−1)XA(b)−Jb,A(N),Jb,A(N)=∑a∈Aa≤N∑j=1⌊N/a⌋bN−ja.

The identity follows by division of 𝑁N by 𝑎a. If 𝐴A is infinite, then Δ𝑏,𝐴(𝑁) >0Δb,A(N)>0, since some 𝑎 ∈𝐴a∈A exceeds 𝑁N. Suppose that 𝑏 ≥2b≥2 is an integer and 𝑋𝐴(𝑏) =𝑝/𝑞XA(b)=p/q, with 𝑝 ∈ℤp∈Z and 𝑞 ≥1q≥1 an integer. Then 𝑞Δ𝑏,𝐴(𝑁)qΔb,A(N) is a positive integer, and hence Δ𝑏,𝐴(𝑁) ≥1/𝑞Δb,A(N)≥1/q. To obtain a contradiction, it therefore suffices to make Δ𝑏,𝐴(𝑁)Δb,A(N) arbitrarily small. Erdős also proposed using fractional parts of powers times the series value [7].

We average over multiples of a modulus divisible by a finite subset of 𝐴A, whose terms in (D) then vanish. For each remaining exponent, the mean contribution over a complete residue period is small when its gcd with the modulus is large. The incomplete period causes the difficulty: its bound lacks the factor 1/𝑎1/a needed to sum over the exponents. A second average, over dyadic lengths, restores this factor. Indeed, an exponent contributes only at lengths that reach it, and the reciprocals of those lengths have a geometrically decreasing sum. Keeping the dependence on the modulus explicit allows both criteria to use the same finite average.

Section 2 proves the weighted estimate. Section 3 introduces divisor covers through a finite example and proves their averaging estimate. Section 4 combines the criteria. We construct the separating supports in Section 5 and discuss the limits of the argument in Section 6. The main argument ends there. Appendix A gives the inherited reciprocal-summable proof. The other appendices collect finite-denominator results and conditional tests for rational membership, a separate question from the support criteria. Neither 1/21/2 nor 1/211/21 is decided by those tests.

An example beyond reciprocal summability

For the support in the introduction, the two sums can be compared layer by layer. Recall that

𝐴⋆={2𝑘𝑚:𝑘≥1, 𝑚 odd, 𝑚≤22𝑘}.A⋆={2km:k≥1, m odd, m≤22k}.

The layers are disjoint, since their elements have different 22-adic valuations. For 𝑟 ≥2r≥2, put

𝑆𝑟=∑𝑚≤2𝑟𝑚 odd1𝑚.Sr=∑m≤2rm odd1m.

Each block 2𝑗 ≤𝑚 <2𝑗+12j≤m<2j+1, 1 ≤𝑗 <𝑟1≤j<r, contains 2𝑗−12j−1 odd integers, with reciprocal sum between 1/41/4 and 1/21/2. Including 𝑚 =1m=1 gives 𝑟/4 ≤𝑆𝑟 ≤𝑟r/4≤Sr≤r. The sum of reciprocals in the 𝑘kth layer is 2−𝑘𝑆2𝑘 ≥1/42−kS2k≥1/4, so ∑𝑎∈𝐴⋆1/𝑎∑a∈A⋆1/a diverges. For 𝑃 ={2}P={2}, its contribution to the weighted sum satisfies

𝑆2𝑘22𝑘−1≤2𝑘22𝑘−1≤21−𝑘.S2k22k−1≤2k22k−1≤21−k.

The last bound uses 22𝑘 −1 ≥22𝑘−122k−1≥22k−1 and 2𝑘 ≥2𝑘2k≥2k. Summation proves (W). The lower bound 1/41/4 in every layer has already excluded reciprocal summability.

A related selection of a term from an average over an arithmetic progression occurs in Duverney–Tachiya [1]. The sparse-coefficient criteria of Kaneko–Suzuki–Tachiya [2] do not apply directly to the divisor counts 𝑐𝐴(𝑛) =#{𝑎 ∈𝐴 :𝑎 ∣𝑛}cA(n)=#{a∈A:a∣n}: for nonempty 𝐴A, these are positive on every multiple of min𝐴minA. The corresponding density calculation, and the distinction between their remote-tail average and our displacement, are given in Section 1.2 of the long record.

The sets of primes for which the weighted sum converges can also be prescribed. Let 𝐸E be a finite set of primes and let UU be an upward-closed family of subsets of 𝐸E containing 𝐸E but not ∅∅. A finite union of the constructions just described has divergent reciprocal sum, and, for every 𝑏 ≥2b≥2 and finite prime set 𝑃P, its weighted sum 𝑊𝑏,𝑃Wb,P is finite exactly when 𝑃 ∩𝐸 ∈UP∩E∈U. Taking 𝑃 =𝐸P=E shows that every infinite subset has an irrational sum at every integer base. The construction is given in Section 1.3 of the long record.

Positive divisor majorants

The weighted criterion treats exponents individually. A divisor cover can take advantage of correlations between several exponents. The relevant quantity is how many members of a finite set divide the same integer.

We shall also use the divisor counts

𝑐𝐴(𝑛)=#{𝑎∈𝐴:𝑎∣𝑛},𝑋𝐴(𝑏)=∑𝑛≥1𝑐𝐴(𝑛)𝑏−𝑛.(6)(6)cA(n)=#{a∈A:a∣n},XA(b)=∑n≥1cA(n)b−n.

Expanding (𝑏𝑎 −1)−1 =∑𝑗≥1𝑏−𝑎𝑗(ba−1)−1=∑j≥1b−aj and interchanging nonnegative sums gives the identity. Although 𝟏𝐴1A takes only the values zero and one, its divisor transform may take larger values, with 0 ≤𝑐𝐴(𝑛) ≤𝜏(𝑛)0≤cA(n)≤τ(n).

A finite divisor set and the cover condition

For finite 𝐹 ⊆ℕ>0F⊆N>0, write 𝑓𝐹(𝑛) =#{𝑎 ∈𝐹 :𝑎 ∣𝑛}fF(n)=#{a∈F:a∣n}. Consider the four exponents 𝐹 ={2,6,10,30}F={2,6,10,30}. If 2 ∤𝑛2∤n, the count is zero. Otherwise each of the primes 33 and 55 that divides 𝑛n doubles the count. Thus

𝑓𝐹(𝑛)=𝟏2∣𝑛(1+𝟏3∣𝑛)(1+𝟏5∣𝑛).fF(n)=12∣n(1+13∣n)(1+15∣n).

𝑓𝐹(𝑛)𝛼=𝟏2∣𝑛+𝑧𝟏6∣𝑛+𝑧𝟏10∣𝑛+𝑧2𝟏30∣𝑛,𝐶=12(1+𝑧3)(1+𝑧5).fF(n)α=12∣n+z16∣n+z110∣n+z2130∣n,C=12(1+z3)(1+z5).

A strict enlargement and finite unions

The union of the two separating supports requires the mixed theorem.

Corollary 5.2 (a support requiring the mixed criterion). There is an infinite positive support 𝑈U with 𝑈 ∉CU∉C and 𝑈 ∉W𝑏U∉Wb for every integer 𝑏 ≥2b≥2, such that 𝑋𝐴(𝑏)XA(b) is irrational for every infinite 𝐴 ⊆𝑈A⊆U and every integer 𝑏 ≥2b≥2.

Proof. Let 𝑈 =𝐸 ∪𝑉U=E∪V, with 𝐸,𝑉E,V as in Proposition 5.1. A cover of 𝑈U is also a cover of 𝐸E, while convergence of the weighted sum over 𝑈U would imply convergence of the sum over 𝑉V for the same prime set, since all summands are nonnegative. Thus 𝑈U belongs to neither individual class. Theorem 4.1 gives irrationality for every infinite subset of 𝑈U at every integer base 𝑏 ≥2b≥2. ◻

For comparison, Tao–Teräväinen prove the full-prime case at base 22 [3]. The paragraph following it states extensions to prime support at every integer base and to full prime-power support at base 22, leaving the modifications to the reader. It does not treat arbitrary infinite thinnings. The proposed thinning extension is not a premise of any theorem here.

Limits of the small-displacement criterion

The small-displacement condition does not cover even every support whose sum is already known to be irrational. For full support we have

Δ2,ℕ>0(𝑁)>(2𝑁−1)∑𝑎>𝑁2−𝑎=1−2−𝑁≥12(𝑁≥1).Δ2,N>0(N)>(2N−1)∑a>N2−a=1−2−N≥12(N≥1).

The full-support value is nevertheless irrational [5]. Thus a proof for arbitrary support would have to use more than this particular family of small displacements. The example leaves other integer linear forms and averaging arguments available.

The logarithmic lower bound is not a converse: replacing a fractional majorant by a logarithmic one need not control averages along the multiples of a prescribed modulus. The counterexample and the bound that remains valid on ordinary initial intervals are proved in Section 13 of the long record; those proofs were first worked out in an AI-assisted note of 17 September 2026. These are statements about finite averages; they do not rule out an irrationality criterion based on other uses of logarithmic divisor counts.

For squarefree support, Duverney and Tachiya’s theorem already gives irrationality. It holds at every base 2𝑗2j, 𝑗 ≥1j≥1, by Corollary 1.2 and Example 1.1 of Duverney and Tachiya [1]. Their corollary covers the 𝑠s-free products of any pairwise coprime sequence of polynomial growth, and they present it as support for the conjecture of Erdős and Graham stated here as Problem 1.1. For the squarefree support with 11 removed, the divisor count is 2𝜔(𝑛) −12ω(n)−1, which is odd for 𝑛 ≥2n≥2. This excludes a first-block-divisibility condition at even bases. Adjoining 11 removes that parity obstruction while changing the sum by a rational number. The argument concerns that normalisation of the certificate, and gives no obstruction to irrationality of the sum. Details and the other known support families appear in the comparison with known support theorems in the long record.

A growth-only criterion gives a different class: if 𝐴 ={𝑐1 <𝑐2 <⋯}A={c1<c2<⋯} and lim sup𝑛𝑐𝑛/2𝑛 =∞lim supncn/2n=∞, then 𝑋𝐴(𝑏)XA(b) is irrational for every integer 𝑏 ≥2b≥2 [8]. The same section of the long record proves the translation from denominator growth and gives examples showing that this class and reciprocal summability are incomparable. The interval-filling constructions in [9] and the freely chosen lacunary denominators of [16] are not constructions of subseries of these fixed Mersenne weights.

Prime-incidence arguments require additional care as well: multiplying all prime exponents by 22 creates positive correlations between their divisibility indicators. The identity and covariance calculation appear at the end of the long record’s discussion of mixed supports. Size conditions alone do not supply that independence.

Algebraic bases on separated supports

The companion Reading eight Erdős problems together, subsection “Divisibility cuts at every algebraic base”, states a transcendence extension based on the number-field Subspace Theorem. Its hypothesis is an infinite set 𝐻H with indices 𝐿𝑗 <𝑀𝑗Lj<Mj, where 𝐿𝑗 →∞Lj→∞ and 𝑀𝑗 −𝐿𝑗 →∞Mj−Lj→∞, such that every 𝑛 ∈𝐻n∈H with 𝑛 ≤𝐿𝑗n≤Lj divides 𝐿𝑗Lj, and every 𝑛 ∈𝐻n∈H with 𝑛 >𝐿𝑗n>Lj is a multiple of 𝑀𝑗Mj. The claimed conclusion is transcendence of ∑𝑛∈𝐵𝑤𝑛/(𝑡𝑛 −1)∑n∈Bwn/(tn−1) for every infinite 𝐵 ⊆𝐻B⊆H, bounded positive integer weights 𝑤𝑛wn and real algebraic 𝑡 >1t>1.

Every divisibility chain has such cuts, as does 𝐻∗ =⋃𝑗𝑁𝑗{1,…,2𝑁𝑗}H∗=⋃jNj{1,…,2Nj} with 𝑁0 =1N0=1 and 𝑁𝑗+1 =2𝑁𝑗lcm⁡(1,…,2𝑁𝑗)Nj+1=2Njlcm⁡(1,…,2Nj). Each block has a reciprocal sum of at least 1/21/2 and contains antichains of unbounded size. The weighted sum for one prime is at most 2𝑡2/(𝑡 −1)32t2/(t−1)3 at every real 𝑡 >1t>1. This connects the example with the weighted criterion, although the separation condition is not asserted for every support satisfying that criterion.

The companion proof is outside this paper and is not a premise of the weighted, cover or mixed theorem. It has two AI proof reviews, no Lean proof of transcendence and no independent human review. No historical priority is asserted for the extension. The case of arbitrary infinite support at base two remains unresolved.

Reciprocal-summable supports

Theorem A.1 (reciprocal-summable supports). Let 𝐴 ⊆ℕ>0A⊆N>0 be infinite. If

∑𝑎∈𝐴1𝑎<∞,∑a∈A1a<∞,

Erdős also discussed weaker conditions [7]. We do not identify our weighted hypothesis with the conditions he suggested.

Here we can take the observation length to infinity while holding the modulus fixed: reciprocal summability supplies a summable bound for all the remaining exponents. We then enlarge the modulus to make each fixed exponent divide it. No common period for the whole infinite support is required.

The order of limits is essential: the observation length tends to infinity with the modulus fixed, and only then does the modulus increase. Reciprocal summability controls both interchanges.

For example, every powerful integer (each prime factor occurs to exponent at least two) has the form 𝑢2𝑣3u2v3. Hence its reciprocal sum is at most 𝜁(2)𝜁(3)ζ(2)ζ(3), and the theorem applies to every infinite subset of the powerful integers. For full perfect-power supports, compare Duverney–Tachiya [1] and the earlier linear-independence results of Luca–Tachiya [13].

Taking all maximal selected exponents proves the order statement; the size bound follows from ord𝐷𝐹⁡(𝑏) ∣𝜑(𝐷𝐹) <𝐷𝐹ordDF⁡(b)∣φ(DF)<DF when 𝐿 ≥2L≥2. The case 𝐹 ={1}F={1} has order one directly.

The unique-valuation argument also permits signs ±1±1 on the finite summands. This signed extension is not included in the formal statement. The required cyclotomic prime-power fact is proved in Section E. The distinction between primes and prime powers is visible in

𝑋{2,3}(2)=1021,𝑋{2,6}(2)=2263.X{2,3}(2)=1021,X{2,6}(2)=2263.

In both examples 22 has multiplicative order six modulo the denominator. The first combines orders two and three; the second retains the order-six prime power 99, although no prime divisor of 6363 has order six. The boundary 𝐹 ={1}F={1} at base two has 𝐷𝐹 =𝐿 =1DF=L=1. These lower denominator bounds give no upper height control for infinite partial sums and do not decide an infinite-support value. Van Assche instead constructs approximants for the full Lambert series and proves both nonvanishing and decay of the associated integer linear forms [14]. That approximation mechanism does not follow from denominator survival alone.

In particular, 1/211/21 is not a finite subseries sum. If it were, the order of 22 modulo 2121 would force every selected exponent to divide 66. The exponent 11 is excluded since its weight is 11. Any sum containing 22 or 33 exceeds 1/211/21, whereas the only nonzero remaining sum is 1/631/63, from the exponent 66. This will distinguish finite and infinite representations in the next appendix.

𝐾𝐴𝑀(𝑀)=∑𝑟≥1𝑐𝐴(𝑀+𝑟)2−𝑟≤2√𝑀+4.KAM(M)=∑r≥1cA(M+r)2−r≤2M+4.

The equality uses the coefficients of the full support 𝐴A on the right: truncation does not change the coefficients through 𝑀M. Hence the existence hypothesis of Theorem D.2 is equivalent to 1/2 ∈A1/2∈A. No compatible sequence of prefixes is required for the forward implication. The existence of the approximating supports remains unproved and would refute Problem 1.1.

Finite families with a shared prefix.

Theorem D.3 (unbounded shared-prefix families represent one half). Suppose that for every 𝑁N there are 𝑀,𝐾M,K with max{𝑁,1} ≤𝑀max{N,1}≤M, 0 ≤𝐾 ≤𝑀0≤K≤M, and a family satisfying all the conditions in the preceding paragraph. Then 𝑋𝐴(2) =1/2XA(2)=1/2 for some infinite set 𝐴 ⊆ℕ>0A⊆N>0.

For each 𝑀M choose the member with terminal carry 11. Its error 2−𝑀2−M tends to zero along unbounded depths, so Theorem D.2 applies. The other shared-prefix conditions are additional requirements of the proposed construction; the compactness argument uses only this one member. No construction at unbounded depths is established here.

The tests above leave three kinds of arithmetic information to be supplied: returns of the actual greedy sequence, finite approximants at unbounded depths, or an exclusion of a possible final skip. The following questions specify those missing inputs.

Problem D.4 (membership of 1/21 in the Mersenne achievement set). For the greedy remainder of 1/211/21, prove that arbitrarily large 𝑁N satisfy

Sources

For Erdős’s reciprocal-summable extension and fractional-part argument, see pp. 222 and 226 of [7]. The periodic theorem [12] is also stated in Luca and Tachiya’s account [11], and Hornich’s strict-tail theorem is proved in Nitecki’s exposition [10]. These expositions are the sources used here for those two results; the original articles were not independently retrieved. The Formal Conjectures file [6] is statement-level prior art, not a proof dependency.

The linked evidence record identifies the exact Lean statements, source revisions and recorded Comparator checks. No such checks were rerun for this revision. The ordinary arguments here have not had independent human review. They include the 𝐴⋆A⋆ calculation, the fresh-prime construction, the signed finite-denominator extension and the proof of Theorem D.1. For the incomparability result, the formal construction of 𝑉V uses a different construction using finite sets of squarefree divisors. The mixed implication is also formalised. The three logarithmic-sampling results in the long record have separate comparison records; these do not constitute human review of the ordinary proofs. No historical priority is claimed for the support comparison. Conditional statements retain their antecedents, and computations retain their finite ranges.

Reproducing the weighted theorem.

The two declarations for Theorem 1.2 are in the public source at commit 91ca3405. That snapshot pins Lean 4.29.1 in lean-toolchain and its Mathlib revision in lake-manifest.json. From a complete checkout, with elan installed, build the two modules with:

lake exe cache get
python3 scripts/lean_fast_build.py --jobs 2 \
  ErdosProblems.Erdos257.PaperCompleteR8.WeightedReturn \
  ErdosProblems.Erdos257.PaperCompleteR8.WeightedHereditaryClaim

The cache download is optional. The modules contain divisibilityWeightedClaim and finitePrimeWeighted_fixedBase_hereditary, respectively; their precise statements and associated checks are linked above.

The supplementary declarations are collected in the long record’s final source section, grouped by support criteria, finite denominators, integer recurrences and achievement sets.
